chapter_theme: Manimekalai finds Aravana Adigal and tells him all that has happened; he tells how Tarai and Virai, Madhavi and Sudhamathi in their former birth, died, laments the decline of the Buddha's dharma and foretells the next Buddha's coming, defers his own teaching until events have run their course, and gives her the dharma of ending hunger, at which she takes up the bowl.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, now holding the bowl Amudhasurabhi
the aged Buddhist teacher of Puhar
the sea goddess who carried Manimekalai to Manipallavam
the guardian goddess of the Buddha's seat on Manipallavam
Manimekalai's mother, Tarai in a former birth
Manimekalai's companion, Virai in a former birth
king of Kachchayam, husband of Tarai and Virai in their former birth
Duchayan's queen, Manimekalai's elder sister in a former birth

manimekalai:12:1-14.unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 14: Manimekalai's reported account of her own doings closes with பெற்றதும் at 14; line 15 opens the goddess's quoted words about Tarai and Virai, which run to 20.
manimekalai:12:1-14.reading: With her two companions Manimekalai asks where Aravana Adigal lives, comes to the dwelling of the white-haired elder whose tongue never falters, bows three times at his feet, praises him, and begins to tell him of the grove, Udayakumaran's words, the goddess carrying her to Manipallavam, the Buddha's seat showing her the birth she had left, and her learning from the goddess of the husband of that birth.
manimekalai:12:1-14.nuance: Her story is given as a list of clauses ending in -ததும் and -வண்ணமும், so the poet retells eleven kaathais in a breath without letting her speak in direct words; the seat is called அறவோன் ஆசனம், the virtuous one's seat, without naming the Buddha.
manimekalai:12:1-14.event: Manimekalai seeks out Aravana Adigal, bows at his feet and begins to recount what has happened to her since the grove.

manimekalai:12:15-30.unit_note: Boundary moved from 15 to 14 at the start: the unit now opens with the goddess's quoted words at 15 and ends with உரைத்தலும் at 30, which closes the whole report begun at 7.
manimekalai:12:15-30.reading: Her report goes on: the goddess told her that her elder sisters of that birth, Tarai and Virai, died when a cruel deed ripened and were reborn as Madhavi and Sudhamathi to be with her, and that she should hear their story from Aravanan; the goddess gave her three mantras and left; Deepathilakai appeared with grace, gave her Aaputhiran's bowl in truth and sent her to hear Aaputhiran's story from the same teacher; and all this she told the ascetic, bowing.
manimekalai:12:15-30.nuance: Both divine speakers send her to Aravanar for the stories behind what they reveal, so the unit sets up the elder as the keeper of the past lives the goddesses only name; the deaths of 16 are blamed on a ripened deed before 43 to 48 say how they happened.
manimekalai:12:15-30.event: Manimekalai tells Aravanar how the goddess revealed Tarai and Virai's rebirth and gave her three mantras, and how Deepathilakai gave her Aaputhiran's bowl and sent her to him.

claims.claim: a cruel deed, when it ripens, brings death and ruin, and those it strikes are reborn among their former kin

manimekalai:12:31-42.reading: Hearing her, the great ascetic is filled with joy upon joy, promises to tell her the two women's story, and begins: besides the day her goddess told of, when he was going to worship the Padapankaya hill, the twin feet of the First Lord that wash away hard deeds, he met Duchayan, king of Kachchayam, in a grove and asked whether all was well with him and his queens.
manimekalai:12:31-42.nuance: ஆதி முதல்வன், the First Lord, is here the Buddha, whose footprints give the hill its name (kaathai 10, 61 to 68); the Kural's first couplet uses a near phrase (ஆதி பகவன்) for its own unnamed first being. Aravanar speaks of the earlier visit as something the goddess already told, so his account adds a second meeting.
manimekalai:12:31-42.event: Aravanar, delighted, begins to tell how on a later pilgrimage to the Padapankaya hill he met King Duchayan and asked after him and his queens.

claims.claim: worship of the First Lord's twin feet washes away hard deeds

manimekalai:12:43-52.reading: The king, broken, told him that Virai, dazed with drink, went heedlessly before a newly captured elephant and was killed, and that Tarai, hearing it, climbed a terrace and fell to her death; Aravanar told him not to grieve over the fruit of old deeds and rose to leave, and now he asks the two women whether they have come back in another costume, like dancers.
manimekalai:12:43-52.nuance: Karma and the women's own acts are both given: line 16 calls the deaths a cruel deed ripening, while 46 names the drink and 48 the leap; Aravanar's consolation at 50 lets the first explain the second without excusing it. The closing image of dancers changing costume (51 to 52) fits Madhavi, a dancer, and makes rebirth a change of dress.
manimekalai:12:43-52.event: Duchayan tells Aravanar that Virai was killed by an elephant while drunk and Tarai threw herself from a terrace; Aravanar consoles him and leaves.

claims.claim: a death that befalls one's own is the fruit of old deeds and is not to be grieved

manimekalai:12:53-70.unit_note: Boundary moved from 68 to 70: the needle-hole simile begun at 66 completes its sense with உண்டு எனச் சொல்லலும் உண்டு at 69 to 70 and the clause யான் சொல்லுதல் தேற்றார் at 70.
manimekalai:12:53-70.reading: Not content with the women's story, Aravanar tells Manimekalai that the dharma the Lord of Dharma taught no longer flourishes: the great road to the endless good state is choked with grass and thorns while the road to the evil states stands open, the dharma is known to exist only as a sun swallowed by mist is known, and as sea water still seeps through a needle-bored hole in a gem, good dharma can still be reached here, though people will not credit him when he says so.
manimekalai:12:53-70.nuance: Line 55 பிறவியும் அறவியும் is hard: read here as 'birth and dharma' that she has come to know, but அறவி is a rare form. The two similes grade the loss: the mist hides the sun without destroying it, and the hole lets in only a trickle, so decline is not extinction.

claims.claim: the dharma the Buddha taught has declined, so the way to release is nearly closed and the way to evil births lies open
even in the decline good dharma can still be attained, though by few

manimekalai:12:71-82.unit_note: Boundaries moved from 69-80 to 71-82: the unit now opens with the clause on worldly people at 71 that leads into the gods' entreaty, and ends with புகூஉம் at 82, which completes the tank-and-sluice simile begun at 79.
manimekalai:12:71-82.reading: Because worldly people will not grasp it, all the gods of the cosmic circle gathered in Tushita and fell begging at the feet of the Great One, so that in one thousand six hundred and sixteen years the great wise one will appear like the sun over a dark world, and after that the measureless dharma will pour gladly into small ears as a great flood enters a tank through a narrow sluice.
manimekalai:12:71-82.nuance: ஈர் எண்ணூற்றோடு ஈர் எட்டு (77) is read as two eight-hundreds and two eights, 1616 years; the text does not say from what point the years are counted. The sluice simile (79 to 82) answers the needle-hole simile of 66 to 68: the same small opening, but now with a flood behind it.

claims.claim: at the gods' entreaty in Tushita a Buddha will be born after 1616 years and his dharma will again fill the world

manimekalai:12:83-103.unit_note: Boundary moved from 81 to 83: lines 81 and 82 complete the sluice simile of the unit before; this unit opens with the gem-and-sunrise simile at 83 and ends with the vow at 103.
manimekalai:12:83-103.reading: When the Buddha-sun rises to clear the dark stain of minds, Aravanar says, sun and moon will shine unharmed, the stars keep their course, the rain will not fail, the earth, winds and sea will yield, cows will feed their calves and fill the pails, beasts and men will lose their fear of each other, the beings of hell and the ghosts will be freed of torment, and no creature will be born hunchbacked, dwarfed, dumb, deaf or deluded; those born then who hear his dharma of grace will pass beyond painful birth, and so he will not forget, in any birth, to praise the feet of the Lord of the Bodhi tree.
manimekalai:12:83-103.nuance: The blessings of 87 to 98 are the old Tamil signs of a just king's reign (unfailing rain, full udders) moved to a Buddha's coming. Aravanar does not expect to escape birth himself before then: his vow is to keep worshipping through every birth until the age of hearing comes.

claims.claim: a Buddha's appearance sets the heavens, the seasons and all creatures right and frees even the beings of hell from torment
those who hear a Buddha's dharma of grace pass beyond painful rebirth

manimekalai:12:104-121.reading: Aravanar tells her that many events will happen in the city because of her and that she will not take up the teaching until they have; that Madhavi and Sudhamathi, having worshipped the Padapankaya hill, will with her worship the Bodhi sage's feet, shed their deeds and go the faultless way; and that since she now holds the great bowl Amudhasurabhi, he gives her one dharma alike in its end for men and gods, ending the disease of hunger; and the girl takes up the bowl to quench the burning hunger of all lives.
manimekalai:12:104-121.nuance: பொருளுரை பொருந்தாய் (107) is read as a deferral: the doctrine will come after the events, and the epic keeps it back until kaathai 29. Feeding the hungry is given first to a renunciant, not to a householder or king, and is called தவப் பெரு நல் அறம், the great good dharma of tapas.
manimekalai:12:104-121.event: Aravanar defers his teaching, foretells Madhavi's and Sudhamathi's release, and gives Manimekalai the dharma of ending hunger; she takes up the bowl.

claims.claim: worship of the Bodhi sage's feet removes the deeds that follow one and leads to the faultless path
ending the hunger of living beings is a dharma whose end is the same for men and for gods

links.note: The goddess says Tarai and Virai were reborn beside Manimekalai because they worshipped at the Padapankaya hill when Aravanar bade them; Aravanar now tells that afterwards one died drunk under an elephant and the other leapt from a terrace.
links.teaches: Held together, the two accounts show the epic letting one act of worship outlast a drunken death and a suicide: the manner of dying does not cancel the merit, which is why the two women now stand beside the heroine.

links.note: The quatrain says that knowing people still do blameworthy things because of deeds done before; the epic calls Virai's drunken death and Tarai's fall the ripening of a cruel deed.
links.teaches: The epic applies the quatrain's explanation to a death and then, at 46 to 48, names the drink and the leap, so a past deed is the cause behind the act while the act itself stays on the record.

gains.a: the epic's bare phrase வெவ் வினை உருப்ப gains a stated mechanism: the old deed works by producing the fault itself
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract puzzle gains a named case in which the blameworthy act is fatal and its doer is reborn

links.note: The couplet asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve when it turns; Aravanar tells a king who has lost both queens not to grieve, since it is the fruit of old deeds.
links.teaches: The couplet grounds equanimity in consistency toward one's own fortune; the epic's monk grounds it in karma and speaks it to a mourner, showing the same counsel turned from self-discipline into consolation for another's loss.

gains.a: Aravanar's curt consolation gains the Kural's argument from consistency, which keeps it from sounding like indifference
gains.b: the couplet gains a hard case: bereavement, where the counsel must be said by one person to another

links.note: Tirumular bids refuge in the shade of the feet of the one God present in all ten directions, so that the sea of deeds will not reach; Aravanar goes to worship the footprints of the First Lord on one hill because they wash away hard deeds.
links.teaches: Both texts make worship of feet dissolve karma, but the Saiva feet are everywhere because their Lord is, while the Buddhist feet are a print left on a particular hill by a teacher of the past, so the shared gesture rests on opposite accounts of where the cleansing power lies.

gains.a: the epic's footprint worship is shown to use a devotional idiom the Saiva texts also use, against which its relic-and-place character stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that the feet are in every direction gains a contrast with a rival tradition whose sacred feet are fixed in one place

links.note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the great sea of births; Aravanar says those who hear the Buddha's dharma pass beyond painful birth and vows to praise the Bodhi Lord's feet in every birth.
links.teaches: The epic names the couplet's unnamed feet as the Buddha's but moves the crossing onto hearing his teaching, and its worshipper expects many more births before that hearing, so the feet become a lifelong devotion rather than the crossing itself.

gains.a: Aravanar's vow gains a reading against the Kural's opening chapter, which shows how much of the shared idiom a Buddhist could take over
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a test case: a reader of another faith who fills the name and changes the means

links.note: Freshly aware of her past birth, Manimekalai hails the Buddha at his seat as a young sun risen over a world that had lost its light; Aravanar foretells the next Buddha as a sun rising to clear the stain of minds.
links.teaches: The sun image moves from praise of a Buddha already come to prophecy of one yet to come, so the epic places its heroine between two dawns, in the age of mist that Aravanar describes at 63 to 65.

links.note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai she will not take up the teaching until the events her presence causes have happened; seventeen kaathais later she asks him for the true doctrine and he begins with the two means of knowledge.
links.teaches: The deferral is kept: the epic withholds its doctrinal core until its heroine has fed the hungry, emptied a prison and heard the other schools, so experience is made the condition of hearing the Buddha's logic.

links.note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who end others' hunger; an ascetic here names ending hunger as the one dharma equal for men and gods and calls it the dharma of tapas.
links.teaches: The epic answers the couplet's ranking by giving the higher strength to a renunciant: with the bowl, the one who has left the household can feed others instead of only enduring hunger, and feeding becomes the ascetic's own discipline.

gains.a: Aravanar's claim gains the Kural's prior ranking of feeding above endurance, which explains why he can call feeding a form of tapas
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and feeder gains a case where one person holds both roles

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: புத்த ஞாயிறு (86); also போதி உரவோன் (111), தரும தலைவன் (57)

source_issues: The kaathai title prints அறவணர்த் தொழுத கதை, not காதை as in the other titles.
Line 55 reads பிறவியும் அறவியும்; அறவி is a rare form and the line's sense is not certain.
Line 121 ends with the closing mark என், as the kaathais do.
